case_study_insert.main_stem: Eastbrook Training (EBT) is a workers' cooperative in the education sector, employing a workforce of 35. Founded in 2015 by Amina Eastbrook, it delivers vocational training units to local employers and operates a flat structure with democratic leadership. EBT plans to invest $480,000 in a virtual-reality simulation workshop, financed by a $260,000 five-year bank loan and $220,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $210,000 a year, a variable cost of $5.00 a unit and a selling price of $11.00, and currently produces 70,000 units a year. Its courses have won two regional awards for employability. EBT faces two problems: equipment downtime has reached 9% and labour turnover among trainers is rising.
case_study_insert.appendix_1_marketing_ops: Training Quality Report, Q1 2026: The simulation workshop delivered 16,500 trainee units last quarter with an assessment re-sit rate of 3.6%, down from 5.8% a year ago. Employer complaints about trainer availability fell from 37 to 18 per month. Average equipment downtime is 9% of scheduled hours. A survey of 380 employers found 69% would pay up to $0.60 more for VR-enhanced courses and 55% check accreditation before commissioning training. Records show 12 of 35 trainers have not completed on-the-job training on the VR rigs; certificated courses cost $840 per trainer.

appendix_2_financial_data.title: Extract from the Statement of Profit or Loss and Capital employed data of Eastbrook Training for the year ended 31 March 2025 ($ '000)

case_study_insert.appendix_3_external_environment: Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank has raised the base interest rate from 4.5% to 5.25%, increasing variable-rate borrowing costs. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 6.1% from $12.90 to $13.69 per hour, adding to wage bills. (3) VR hardware and broadband input costs have risen 13.2% year-on-year, training-services inflation is 5.9%, and employer spending on staff development grew 3.3% over the same period.

questions.question_text: EBT plans to fund part of its $480,000 VR workshop with a $260,000 five-year bank loan. Explain two advantages for EBT of using retained profit rather than the bank loan.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Retained profit has no interest charges or fixed repayments, so the $220,000 from earlier surpluses protects the cooperative's cash flow while it meets fixed costs of $210,000 a year. Cash preserved can absorb the 13.2% rise in VR hardware and broadband costs without lifting the $11.00 price, keeping the $6.00 contribution on 70,000 units.

Point 2: Retained profit needs no security, so the $480,000 workshop is not exposed to repossession if employer orders fall. It also preserves member control, since no lender can set conditions on how the cooperative is run. Because funds are already internal, EBT can act at once to replace the equipment behind 9% downtime and tackle rising trainer turnover. Fixed costs of $210,000 a year are already a heavy commitment for 35 trainers, and the cooperative's two regional awards depend on reliable delivery that debt service could jeopardise, whereas internal funds can be released without lender approval.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage of retained profit over a bank loan (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation applied to EBT, its workshop, costs and cooperative structure.

questions.question_text: EBT is promoting its new VR-enhanced courses. Consider advertising in regional business newspapers, sponsoring a large employer skills fair, or targeted social media and email marketing to local employers. Which should EBT choose? Justify your recommendation.
questions.model_answer:
Regional business newspapers: Newspaper adverts would reach local managers and build awareness cheaply, but readership is declining and a general audience includes many firms that do not buy vocational training. For a 35-staff cooperative investing $480,000, much of the spend is wasteful and the static message cannot demonstrate the VR equipment.

Employer skills fair sponsorship: A major skills fair would put EBT in front of the exact HR managers who commission training and allow live VR demonstrations, supporting the 55% of surveyed employers who check accreditation. It is prestigious but a very expensive one-off; with 380 employers surveyed and 16,500 units delivered last quarter, one fair alone cannot sustain 70,000 units a year.

Targeted social media and email marketing: Digital marketing to local employers can show VR footage to the 69% who would pay $0.60 more, be updated as the 9% downtime falls, and deliver measurable enquiries at low cost. The limitation is that busy managers may ignore messages and training purchases rely on relationships, so follow-up calls would be needed. A low cost per enquiry matters when fixed costs already run at $210,000 a year.

Recommendation: EBT should choose targeted social media and email marketing, backed by a small presence at the skills fair. It reaches the 69% willing to pay $0.60 more cheaply and can run continuously for 70,000 units, unlike a single event. Newspapers are rejected as declining and untargeted; major fair sponsorship is rejected as too costly and one-off for a cooperative already servicing a $260,000 loan.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies promotional options with limited reference to EBT's survey or courses.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Discusses advantages and disadvantages of at least two options in the context of EBT with some judgement.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Evaluates all three options with a justified recommendation that explains why newspapers and skills-fair sponsorship are rejected.

questions.question_text: EBT has a flat structure with democratic leadership and rising labour turnover among trainers. Explain two benefits for EBT of introducing job rotation for its trainers.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Job rotation lets the 35 trainers switch between VR simulation delivery, assessment and course design, breaking the monotony that contributes to rising labour turnover. Varied work satisfies esteem needs in Maslow's hierarchy and builds a wider skill base, helping reduce the 12 of 35 trainers still without VR rig training and the 3.6% re-sit rate.

Point 2: Rotation spreads cover when equipment downtime reaches 9%, so a fault in one area does not stop all delivery, protecting the 16,500 units delivered last quarter. In a flat democratic structure, trainers can also share ideas about the $840 certificated courses, making training more relevant and reducing the disruption caused by losing experienced staff. Rotation also spreads the 12 untrained trainers across rigs so they learn from colleagues without a costly course, and it fits a democratic culture where members expect a say in how work is organised, addressing rising labour turnover directly.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid benefit of job rotation (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual development linked to EBT's turnover, downtime, training and structure.

questions.question_text: EBT must train 12 of its 35 trainers on the new VR rigs. Consider on-the-job training or certificated external courses costing $840 per trainer. Which should EBT choose? Justify your decision.
questions.model_answer:
On-the-job training: Learning on the VR rigs is tailored to EBT's own workshop and costs no fees, keeping the 12 trainers productive while they learn. That protects the 16,500 units delivered last quarter and the improvement in re-sit rate from 5.8% to 3.6%. Drawbacks are that mentor trainers deliver fewer sessions, local habits may spread, and there is no certificate to satisfy the 55% of employers who check accreditation.

Certificated external courses: At $840 per trainer, certificating all 12 costs $10,080 ($840 x 12), affordable against the $480,000 investment, and gives recognised qualifications that appeal to accreditation-conscious employers. However, it removes 12 of 35 trainers from delivery temporarily, worsening the 9% downtime pressure, and generic content may not match EBT's exact VR rigs, so follow-up coaching would still be required. The $10,080 must be weighed against 9% equipment downtime, which already cuts into the 16,500 units delivered last quarter. Certificates would help with the 55% of employers who check accreditation, but only a few trainers need them immediately.

Decision: EBT should choose on-the-job training first, adding certificates for senior trainers later. It is cheaper, rig-specific and avoids losing capacity while downtime is 9% and turnover is rising; full external training is rejected because the $10,080 and the loss of 12 trainers would disrupt the 70,000-unit target, and accreditation can be added once the workshop is established, spreading the cost across financial years after one term's review, while senior trainers coach the rest on site; a short external course for two senior trainers would still secure the accreditation signal valued by 55% of employers.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Describes the two training methods with little application to EBT.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the benefits and drawbacks of each method in the context of EBT's costs, capacity and staffing.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensive evaluation of both methods with a justified decision that rejects the alternative and refers to cost, disruption and equipment relevance.

questions.question_text: Calculate and explain how EBT's management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.

sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Break-even output = Fixed costs ÷ Contribution per unit. Substitution: $210,000 ÷ ($11.00 − $5.00) = $210,000 ÷ $6.00 = 35,000 units. Answer: break-even output is 35,000 units a year.
Formula: Contribution per unit = Selling price − Variable cost per unit. Substitution: $11.00 − $5.00 = $6.00. Answer: contribution per unit is $6.00.

sub_parts.question_text: Explain four ways EBT's management can use this cost and break-even data.
sub_parts.model_answer:
1. Compare the 35,000-unit break-even output with 70,000 actual units to find a margin of safety of 35,000 units (70,000 − 35,000), showing the $480,000 workshop can absorb a fall in employer demand.
2. Use the $6.00 contribution to assess the survey: at 70,000 units a $0.60 premium would add $42,000 (70,000 x $0.60), funding the $840 trainer certificates.
3. Check that contribution covers fixed costs of $210,000 and interest on the $260,000 loan before expanding, so finance costs do not raise break-even.
4. Benchmark average total cost of $8.00 ($210,000 ÷ 70,000 + $5.00) each quarter to detect waste from 9% equipment downtime and judge whether 13.2% input-cost inflation is absorbed.

questions.model_answer: (i) Break-even output = 35,000 units | (ii) Contribution per unit = $6.00 | (iii) Four contextual uses: a margin of safety of 35,000 units against 70,000 output; a $0.60 premium adding $42,000; covering $210,000 fixed costs and $260,000 loan interest; and unit-cost benchmarking at $8.00 to track 13.2% input inflation.

working_marks: 1 mark for the correct formula and accurate numerical answer in (i) and (ii); 1 mark per valid applied point in (iii).

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 2, evaluate EBT's financial performance by calculating the gross profit margin, profit margin and ROCE for 2024 and 2025. Has EBT's financial performance improved? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Calculations:
Gross Profit Margin 2024 = 40.0%
Gross Profit Margin 2025 = 43.0%
Profit Margin 2024 = 14.0%
Profit Margin 2025 = 15.0%
ROCE 2024 = 21.0%
ROCE 2025 = 22.5%

Detailed workings: Gross profit of $600,000 on revenue of $1,500,000 in 2024 gives 600 ÷ 1,500 = 40.0%; in 2025 gross profit of $774,000 on $1,800,000 gives 774 ÷ 1,800 = 43.0%. Operating profit of $210,000 ÷ $1,500,000 = 14.0% in 2024 and $270,000 ÷ $1,800,000 = 15.0% in 2025. The return on capital employed divides operating profit by capital employed: $210,000 ÷ $1,000,000 = 21.0% and $270,000 ÷ $1,200,000 = 22.5%. Cost of sales of $900,000 and $1,026,000 reconciles exactly with gross profit in both years.

Evaluation: All three measures improved. The increase from 40.0% to 43.0% shows more revenue retained after direct costs, as revenue grew $300,000 while cost of sales rose only $126,000, so most of the revenue gain was retained as gross profit. Operating profitability rose from 14.0% to 15.0%, suggesting the cooperative controlled overheads as units grew. The return on capital improved from 21.0% to 22.5%, so the $1,200,000 capital employed is being used more efficiently, which supports the $480,000 workshop. Interest payable fell from $24,000 to $20,000, reducing the drag on surpluses.

Conclusion: EBT's financial performance has improved. Every margin rose, the return on capital strengthened and interest payable fell, leaving the cooperative better able to service the $260,000 loan. Management should still reduce 9% equipment downtime and rising trainer turnover, which could undermine these gains.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: States financial figures or changes without accurate ratio calculations.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Accurately calculates the three measures for both years with contextual analysis of the trend.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Accurate calculations for both years with detailed evaluation of revenue, cost of sales, capital employed and interest movements and a justified conclusion on whether performance improved.

questions.question_text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for EBT of offering VR-enhanced courses.
questions.model_answer:
Advantage: VR courses match the survey evidence that 69% of employers would pay up to $0.60 more and 55% check accreditation. At 70,000 units a $0.60 premium could add $42,000 (70,000 x $0.60), protecting the $6.00 contribution per unit against 13.2% input-cost inflation and supporting the $480,000 workshop. The two regional awards show employers already value innovation, so VR may help win work from more of the 380 surveyed firms.

Disadvantage: VR hardware and broadband costs raise the $5.00 variable cost per unit, and 9% equipment downtime already disrupts delivery, so margins could be squeezed if the $0.60 premium is not widely accepted. With rising trainer turnover and 12 of 35 trainers untrained on the rigs, a hardware fault or skills gap would also push up the 3.6% re-sit rate and damage the cooperative's award-winning reputation. Without a breakdown of the $5.00 variable cost, this margin pressure can only be judged qualitatively.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for a valid advantage and 1 mark for a valid disadvantage.
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual development linked to EBT's survey data, costs and workshop.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the interest rate rise to 5.25%, the 6.1% minimum wage increase and the 13.2% rise in input costs will affect EBT. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Interest rate rise (4.5% to 5.25%): If EBT's $260,000 five-year bank loan is variable-rate, the 0.75 percentage-point rise adds 0.75% x $260,000 = $1,950 a year (0.0075 x $260,000), small alongside fixed costs of $210,000, and zero if the loan is fixed. Higher rates may also make employers trim development budgets, but EBT can largely remove the direct risk by fixing the rate.

Minimum wage increase (6.1%, to $13.69 an hour): With a workforce of 35 and output of 70,000 units, labour productivity is 70,000 ÷ 35 = 2,000 units per worker. The insert provides no hours worked or individual pay rates, so an annual wage total cannot be invented; the sound test is whether each trainer sustains about 2,000 units. With labour turnover rising, any productivity fall would lift unit labour costs and shrink the $6.00 contribution.

Input-cost inflation (13.2% in VR hardware and broadband): The insert states a $5.00 variable cost per unit without decomposing it, so only an illustrative bound is defensible. If the whole $5.00 rose 13.2%, that is 13.2% x $5.00 = $0.66 per unit; across 70,000 units that is about $46,200 a year (70,000 x $0.66). Even a smaller $0.50 rise would cost $35,000 a year (70,000 x $0.50), pulling contribution from $6.00 to about $5.50.

Conclusion: The 13.2% rise in input costs will have the greatest impact. It touches all 70,000 units and directly erodes the $6.00 contribution supporting the $480,000 workshop, and at up to about $46,200 a year it far outweighs the conditional $1,950 interest cost. The wage rise matters but cannot be quantified from the insert and depends on 2,000-unit productivity holding, while interest exposure is small and fixable. EBT should negotiate hardware deals and recover part of the increase through the $0.60 VR premium.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the external changes with limited application to EBT.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two external changes on EBT's costs, revenue or financing in context.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three changes with a justified judgement that input-cost inflation has the greatest impact and why the other two are smaller, with arithmetic shown from insert figures.
